body.estimand_functional: \Gamma_{\rho,w,m}(\mu)=\min\{\min_{J\in\mathcal J_m:h\notin J}Q_J^{\mathrm E}(\rho,\mu),\min_{J\in\mathcal J_m:h\in J}\min_{j\in J\setminus\{h\}}Q_{J,j}^{\mathrm T}(\rho,\mu)\},\quad \max_{2\le m\le K-1}\sup_{0<\rho<1}\inf_{\mu:|\arg\max_i\mu_i|=1}\Gamma_{\rho,w,m}(\mu)/I_w(\mu)=G_{\mathrm{multi}},\quad \sup_{D\in\mathfrak D_2^{\mathrm{all,multi}}}\inf_{\mu:|\arg\max_i\mu_i|=1}\Gamma_D(\mu)/I_w(\mu)\stackrel{?}{=}G_{\mathrm{multi}}

sampling_model.design: A fixed-budget two-batch rule assigns the first fraction \(\rho\) according to known variance-only weights \(w\), retains the \(m\) largest first-batch empirical means, and assigns the remainder proportionally among those survivors; both \(m\) and \(\rho\) are certified design choices.
sampling_model.units: For each arm, experimental outcomes are independent Gaussian draws with a fixed unknown mean and a known finite positive arm-specific variance.
sampling_model.treatment: There are \(K\ge3\) mutually exclusive treatment arms, and exactly one treatment is assigned to each sampled unit.
sampling_model.overlap: Every arm has a positive first-batch allocation because \(w\) is interior, and every retained arm has a positive second-batch allocation because \(0<\rho<1\) and \(W_J>0\).
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: There is no nuisance estimation in the selected kernel because the variance vector is known; unknown-variance adaptation remains outside scope.

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: Their sufficient-condition theorem proves strict large-deviation dominance of batched arm elimination over uniform allocation under a common Gaussian variance; literal model-and-comparator overlap is this paper's common-variance subclass, while the broader connection is the BAE motif.
The GNA-EBA allocation maximizes the worst equal-gap Gaussian exponent using known heterogeneous variances.
An adaptive-sampling large-deviation technique supplies one-sided bounds for empirical recommendations.
SHVar has a finite-budget exponential upper bound under known heterogeneous reward variances.
No fixed-budget algorithm uniformly matches the stronger mean-aware static-oracle exponent for \(K\ge3\) in a regular one-parameter natural exponential family.
Three batches attain asymptotically optimal fixed-confidence sample complexity.

body.tldr: For every \(K\ge3\) and every known finite positive Gaussian variance vector, a fully specified proportional two-batch rule can retain any top \(m\in\{2,\ldots,K-1\}\) first-batch arms and reallocate the remaining budget proportionally among them. The exact Gaussian exponent is a finite minimum over \(\binom{K-1}{m}\) best-exclusion and \((m-1)\binom{K-1}{m-1}\) terminal branches. Weighted projections and separated matching witnesses give \(L_m(\rho)=\min\{\rho C_m,1+(1-\rho)\eta_{K-m}\}\), the unique timing \(\rho_m^\star=(1+\eta_{K-m})/(C_m+\eta_{K-m})\), and gain \(G_m>1\). Enumerating \(m\) yields the certified design \(G_{\mathrm{multi}}=\max_m G_m\); in the common-variance subclass its optimal survivor count is of order \(\sqrt K\) and the gain tends to two. The connection to Imbens, Qin, and Wager is the batched-arm-elimination motif; literal distributional and comparator overlap is the common-variance subclass.

project_justification.gap: The closest design-motif result, Imbens, Qin, and Wager's common-variance batched arm-elimination theorem, gives sufficient conditions for strict large-deviation dominance over uniform allocation. It does not give the heteroskedastic survivor-set contraction, exact terminal-branch equality, optimal retained-arm count, or dominance over Kato's variance-aware equal-gap maximin allocation.
project_justification.niche: The proportional top-\(m\) family keeps the BAE motif while treating the number of survivors, the first-batch fraction, and known arm-specific variances as explicit design inputs. Literal overlap with the Imbens--Qin--Wager setting is confined to equal variances.
project_justification.fill: The project proves the exact survivor-set Gaussian branch formula, reduces every best-exclusion coefficient to at most \(K\) one-dimensional quadratic pieces, constructs matching elimination and terminal witnesses, optimizes timing for each \(m\), and then performs the finite discrete optimization over survivor counts.

body.related_work: Imbens, Qin, and Wager are the closest design-motif comparator: under a common Gaussian variance, their batched arm-elimination result gives sufficient conditions for strict large-deviation dominance over uniform allocation. The present paper literally overlaps that setting only in its common-variance subclass; beyond it, arm-specific variances alter both the baseline allocation and every survivor-set projection. Kato derives the generalized Neyman static comparator from a worst equal-gap Gaussian experiment, without asserting pointwise admissibility away from equal gaps. The theorem here strictly improves that variance-aware comparator, derives exact coupled branch exponents, and optimizes the number of survivors. Wang, Tzeng, and Proutiere provide an adaptive large-deviation upper-bound technique, while their completeness caveat leaves room for the finite-branch equality proved here. Lalitha et al. show how known heterogeneous variances alter elimination allocations and provide finite-budget bounds; their stagewise analysis informs, but does not imply, the survivor-set certificate. Goldberger's impossibility for matching a stronger mean-aware oracle is consistent with this paper because \(w\) depends only on variances. Jin et al. optimize a different fixed-confidence batched criterion, whereas this paper solves an exact fixed-budget robust-gain game in the proportional two-batch class.
body.technical_internal_limitation: The generalized quantity \(B_{T,m}\) is a conservative upper certificate for the adaptive design's error probability, not an equality at finite \(T\). Comparing two upper certificates does not establish finite-sample risk dominance. The strict comparator claim is therefore an exact large-deviation-exponent statement; \(B_{T,m}\) is useful for planning under specified mean scenarios and for software regression tests.
body.honest_scope: The exact exponent, top-\(m\) projection inequality, matching survivor-set witnesses, timing optimum, discrete optimization over \(m\), equal-variance reduction, and rounded Chernoff certificate are proved for independent Gaussian streams with known finite positive variances and a unique best arm. The old eliminate-one result is the \(m=K-1\) reduction. The genuinely unrestricted residual class is now \(\mathfrak D_2^{\mathrm{all,multi}}\): it jointly ranges over the survivor count, every interior first-batch allocation, and every branch-specific interior survivor allocation. The proved proportional family embeds in this class and certifies a lower bound of \(G_{\mathrm{multi}}\), but a matching allocation-uniform upper saddle certificate is open. The former unrestricted-allocation eliminate-one class \(\mathfrak D_2^{\mathrm{all}}\) remains only the nested \(m=K-1\) subquestion. Unknown-variance adaptation, non-Gaussian rewards, variance ratios changing with budget, \(K=2\), and finite-sample risk dominance are outside the theorem.
body.interpretation: Retaining more arms makes erroneous exclusion of the best arm exponentially harder, through \(C_m\), but spreads the second-batch reallocation across a larger survivor weight, through \(\eta_{K-m}\). The certified schedule balances these two explicit failure modes, and \(m^\star\) chooses the best balance before outcomes are observed.
